name: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
aliases: congenital absence of the vas deferens
congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens

reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Congenital absence of the vas deferens is an important cause of obstructive azoospermia in which the vasa cannot be palpated in the scrotum
It classically produces a low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative ejaculate because the seminal vesicles are frequently absent or hypoplastic alongside the missing vasa
Spermatogenesis is usually normal, so testicular volume and follicle-stimulating hormone are typically preserved, confirming an obstructive rather than a productive problem
The bilateral form is strongly linked to mutations in the cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene, and affected men may represent a mild phenotype of cystic fibrosis
Both the man and his partner should undergo cystic-fibrosis gene testing, with genetic counselling before conception because of the risk of an affected child
The unilateral form and some bilateral cases are associated with ipsilateral renal anomalies, so upper-tract imaging is recommended, particularly when cystic-fibrosis mutations are not found
Fertility is achievable through surgical sperm retrieval from the epididymis or testis combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
The diagnosis is largely clinical, resting on the absence of palpable vasa, and is supported by seminal analysis and imaging
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens arises from failure of development of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct derivatives, so the vasa deferentia, and often the distal epididymis and seminal vesicles, are absent or rudimentary. Because sperm cannot pass from the testis into the ejaculate, the result is obstructive azoospermia with intact testicular sperm production. Most bilateral cases are caused by mutations in the cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene, placing the condition within the spectrum of cystic-fibrosis-related disease; the same gene defects that impair chloride transport disrupt Wolffian duct development. A subset, more often unilateral, is instead associated with abnormal embryological development of the mesonephric duct and coexisting renal agenesis or ectopia, reflecting the shared origin of the reproductive and upper urinary tracts.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of obstructive azoospermia such as acquired vasal or epididymal obstruction
Retrograde ejaculation producing low ejaculate volume
Young syndrome with obstructive azoospermia and sinopulmonary disease
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal examination confirming non-palpable vasa deferentia
Semen analysis showing low volume with acidic pH and absent fructose
Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, and testosterone, expected to be normal
Cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene testing of the man and his partner
Renal tract ultrasound to detect associated renal agenesis or ectopia
Transrectal ultrasound to assess the seminal vesicles and distal ducts
Diagnostic confirmation of intact spermatogenesis at the time of sperm retrieval
redFlags: Detection of cystic-fibrosis gene mutations in the partner, substantially raising the risk of an affected child
An associated solitary or ectopic kidney requiring surveillance
Features suggesting overt cystic fibrosis such as recurrent respiratory disease
Findings inconsistent with obstruction that suggest an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: General health is usually unaffected in the absence of overt cystic fibrosis, and because spermatogenesis is intact, fatherhood is readily achievable with surgical sperm retrieval and intracytoplasmic sperm injection; the principal consideration is the genetic risk to offspring, which is addressed through partner testing and counselling.
pitfalls: Failing to palpate for the vasa and thus missing the diagnosis in an azoospermic man
Omitting cystic-fibrosis gene testing of the man and, crucially, his partner before assisted conception
Neglecting renal imaging, particularly in cases without cystic-fibrosis mutations
Misclassifying the low-volume ejaculate as ejaculatory duct obstruction without checking for palpable vasa
Proceeding to assisted reproduction without genetic counselling about the risk to children
references: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
